statement: In general-population cohorts followed over time and in first-episode case-control studies, people who use cannabis, compared with people who do not, are more likely to develop psychotic symptoms or a psychotic disorder, and the association is stronger with more frequent use. Few sources give absolute risks. As a base rate, 362 of 50,087 men conscripted in Sweden in 1969 (about 7 in 1,000, editors' calculation) were diagnosed with schizophrenia by about age 45, whatever their cannabis use (as tabulated in a narrative review, Gage et al., 2016); in the same cohort, as tabulated in a meta-analysis, 215 of 36,429 men who had never used cannabis by conscription (about 6 in 1,000) and 28 of 731 who had used it more than 50 times (about 38 in 1,000) were later admitted to hospital with schizophrenia, crude proportions with nothing adjusted (editors' calculation; Marconi et al., 2016). A systematic review of seven cohorts published to 2006 (Moore et al., 2007; AMSTAR 2 low confidence) pooled each cohort's own adjusted odds ratio (about 60 confounders across the studies, among them other substance use, personality traits, intellectual ability and other mental health problems): 1.41 (95% CI 1.20 to 1.65; I² 19%) for any later psychotic outcome, mostly self-reported or interview-rated symptoms, after ever use (past-year use in one cohort) against never use; 2.09 (1.54 to 2.84; I² 44%) for each cohort's most frequent use (from more than 50 lifetime occasions to weekly or daily use or dependence) against no use, three of the six estimates not adjusted for other drug use; and 2.58 (1.08 to 6.13; I² 67%) for a psychotic disorder after ever use in the three cohorts with that outcome, or 1.82 (1.01 to 3.30) without the most heterogeneous one. Across the seven cohorts, adjustment removed on average about 45% of the crude excess odds (10% to 80% by cohort, for exposure contrasts the review does not state). Of three cohorts published after that review, as summarized by Gage et al. (2016), the association did not remain after adjustment in two (Zurich; ALSPAC, 1.12, 0.76 to 1.65, after adjustment for tobacco and other illicit drugs, an adjustment the original authors discussed as possible over-adjustment, the association having remained after adjustment for pre-birth and childhood factors), while a Californian hospital cohort reported a hazard ratio of 8.16 (5.08 to 13.12) for later admission with schizophrenia after a hospital diagnosis of cannabis use disorder, against people admitted with appendicitis. A meta-analysis of crude counts from ten studies (Marconi et al., 2016; AMSTAR 2 critically low) found the odds of a psychosis-related outcome rising with rank on each study's own scale of use: a fitted odds ratio of 3.90 (2.84 to 5.34; I² 82%) for the single most-exposed person on each scale and 3.40 (2.55 to 4.54) for the middle of the top fifth, against no use (never use in most studies, no use in the past year or at a given age in some), with nothing adjusted and with category-level odds that did not rise steadily in several studies; five of its six cohorts are reports the 2007 review also pooled. In two first-episode case-control studies from one team, daily use as the person's most consistent pattern over the lifetime was reported more often by people with a psychotic disorder than by controls: fully adjusted odds ratio 3.2 (2.2 to 4.1) against never or occasional use (901 cases and 1,237 population controls at 11 sites in Europe and Brazil; adjusted for age, gender, ethnicity, education, employment, tobacco and other drugs; Di Forti et al., 2019) and 3.04 against never use (410 inpatients and 370 controls recruited by advertisement in south London; adjusted also for alcohol; Di Forti et al., 2015), whereas occasional use was not associated (0.84 and 0.96 for low- and high-potency types at the 11 sites; 0.58 for less-than-weekly use in south London), ever use only weakly (1.3, 1.1 to 1.6) or not at all (0.93), and current use at the 11 sites not after full adjustment (1.1, 0.9 to 1.5). Whether starting young adds risk beyond the amount used was not shown: the cohort review found no robust evidence that it does (Moore et al., 2007), and at the 11 sites first use at 15 or younger had a fully adjusted odds ratio of 1.6 (1.1 to 2.1) against never use while the daily-use estimate changed little (3.1) when age at first use was added. Other absolute figures in the reviews are statements or calculations rather than measurements: the 2007 review puts lifetime risk of chronic psychotic disorders with regular use below 3% without showing how (Moore et al., 2007); Hall (2015) gives as its best estimate a doubling from about 7 to 14 in 1,000 with regular use, which applies the relative estimate to a base rate as if it were causal; and Gage et al. (2016) give a lifetime risk of schizophrenia of about 2% with regular use if the association is causal. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: In studies that followed young people for years, those who had used cannabis were more likely to have psychotic symptoms or a psychotic illness later than those who had not, and the link was stronger for those who used it most often, such as daily. In a large Swedish study, about 7 in 1,000 men were diagnosed with schizophrenia by about age 45, whatever their cannabis use. In the same study, about 6 in 1,000 men who had never used cannabis and about 38 in 1,000 who had used it more than 50 times later went to hospital with schizophrenia, before other differences between them were taken into account. In two studies of people with a first episode of psychosis, using cannabis only now and then was not linked to psychosis. Part of the link shrank when other differences between people were taken into account, and these studies cannot show that cannabis caused it.
population: Adolescents and adults in general-population cohorts in the USA, Germany, the Netherlands, the UK, Sweden (men conscripted in 1969), New Zealand and Switzerland; ten observational studies pooled from crude counts; and people presenting with a first episode of psychosis, with controls from the same areas, in south London (2005 to 2011) and at 11 sites in the UK, the Netherlands, France, Spain, Italy and Brazil (2010 to 2015)
exposure: Self-reported cannabis use as each study defined it: ever use (past-year use in one cohort); each cohort's most frequent use category (more than 50 lifetime occasions, weekly or daily use, or dependence); rank on each study's own ordinal scale of use; in the case-control studies, the lifetime frequency of the person's most consistent pattern (occasional, weekends or more than weekly, daily)
comparator: People in the same cohorts who had never used cannabis or did not use it (in the crude meta-analysis, no use meant never use in most studies but no use in the past year or at a given age in some); in the case-control studies, controls without psychosis, with never use, or never or only occasional use, as the reference group stated
outcome: Later psychotic symptoms or experiences (mostly self-reported or interview-rated, without a requirement of impaired functioning), psychotic disorder (schizophreniform disorder, a needs-based diagnosis or hospital admission for schizophrenia) and, in the case-control studies, a first episode of psychotic disorder (ICD-10 F20 to F33)
magnitude: Moore et al. 2007 (7 cohorts; random-effects pooling of each cohort's adjusted odds ratio): any psychotic outcome, ever vs never use, 1.41 (1.20–1.65), I² 19.2%; most frequent use vs none, 2.09 (1.54–2.84), I² 44.1% (1.92, 1.50–2.47, without NEMESIS); psychotic disorder, ever use, 3 cohorts, 2.58 (1.08–6.13), I² 66.9% (1.82, 1.01–3.30, without NEMESIS); adjustment attenuated crude estimates by about 45% on average (10% to 80%; exposure contrast per cohort not stated). Later cohorts as summarized by Gage et al. 2016: ALSPAC 1.12 (0.76–1.65) after full adjustment; Zurich lost after adjustment; California HR 8.16 (5.08–13.12). Marconi et al. 2016 (10 studies, 66,816 people, crude counts): fitted OR 3.90 (2.84–5.34) for the most-exposed rank vs no use, I² 82%; 3.40 (2.55–4.54) for the median of the top 20%; 1.97 (1.68–2.31) for the median person who had used. Di Forti et al. 2019 (901 cases, 1,237 controls; fully adjusted): daily use vs never or occasional 3.2 (2.2–4.1); more than once a week 1.4 (1.0–2.0); occasional use vs never 0.84 (low potency) and 0.96 (high potency); ever use 1.3 (1.1–1.6); current use 1.1 (0.9–1.5); first use at 15 or younger vs never 1.6 (1.1–2.1). Di Forti et al. 2015 (410 cases, 370 controls; adjusted, against never use): every day 3.04 (printed 1.91–7.76, an interval centred on 3.85 rather than 3.04; with the printed p = 0.020 its lower limit would be about 1.19, editors' calculation), weekends 1.04, less than weekly 0.58 (0.25–1.32), ever use 0.93 (0.67–1.52 as printed; this interval implies p of about 0.73 rather than the printed 0.569, editors' calculation). Absolute: Swedish conscripts, 362 of 50,087 diagnosed with schizophrenia by about age 45, about 7 in 1,000 (editors' calculation; all levels of use); crude, admission with schizophrenia, 215 of 36,429 with no use (about 6 in 1,000) and 28 of 731 with more than 50 occasions (about 38 in 1,000) (editors' calculation from Marconi et al.'s Table 1; unadjusted). Statements and illustrations: lifetime risk of chronic psychotic disorder with regular use below 3%, no derivation (Moore et al., 2007); 7 rising to 14 in 1,000 with regular use, applying a doubling (Hall, 2015); about 2% lifetime risk with regular use if causal (Gage et al., 2016).

risk_of_bias.note: Cohorts (card sc_moore_2007, AMSTAR 2 low confidence): self-reported exposure, each cohort's own adjustment set, three of the six top-category estimates not adjusted for other drug use, and symptom measures in two cohorts that cannot separate intoxication. The rank meta-analysis (sc_marconi_2016, critically low) adjusts for nothing. The case-control studies are at high (sc_di_forti_2019) and very high (sc_di_forti_2015) risk of bias: confounders such as family history unmeasured, exposure recalled after onset and, in south London, volunteer controls. Adjustment alone removed about 45% of the crude excess odds, so residual confounding could change the size of the estimates materially.

inconsistency.note: The direction is consistent: six of seven ever-use estimates above 1 (I² 19%), every top-rank estimate above 1 in the crude meta-analysis, and daily use associated in both case-control studies. Heterogeneity is larger for the disorder estimate (67%) and the crude rank estimate (82%), and two later cohorts were null after adjustment; these differences follow different exposure, outcome and adjustment choices and are reported rather than rated down.

indirectness.note: Worded for the outcomes measured (symptoms or disorder) and for each study's own definition of frequent use; no estimate is applied to a stated number of days of use.

imprecision.note: The ever-use and top-category pools are precise; the disorder estimate is wide (1.08 to 6.13) and is reported with its interval.

publication_bias.note: Egger tests in both meta-analyses found no small-study signal, each with little power (cards sc_moore_2007 and sc_marconi_2016); not rated down.

large_effect.note: Adjusted estimates are about 1.4 for ever use and about 2 for the top categories; the 3.90 is crude. Not applicable.

dose_response.note: Not upgraded: the top categories differ between cohorts, half are not adjusted for other drug use, the pooled gradient across ten studies is crude and does not rise steadily within several of them, and a gradient of use also carries gradients of confounders. With the evidence already rated down for risk of bias, a strict reading does not upgrade; with the upgrade the rating would be low.

plausible_confounding.note: Residual confounding would more plausibly raise than lower these estimates (Gage et al., 2016); no upgrade.

grade.reasoning: Observational, starts low; down one for risk of bias: very low. Rated as worded, an association; whether it is causal is the separate, contested question (see the answer on whether cannabis causes psychosis). Status replicated: several independent cohorts point the same way (CHDS, Dunedin, ECA, EDSP and the Swedish conscripts), and daily use is associated in both case-control studies. Overlapping sources are counted once: five of the six cohorts in the crude meta-analysis are reports that Moore et al. pooled, and its London case-control data are the sample of Di Forti et al. (2015); Gage et al. (2016) restate Moore et al.'s pooled figures, and their informal re-pooling with two later cohorts is not used because it cannot be reproduced from the estimates the review prints (card sc_gage_2016); Hall (2015) restates Moore et al.'s figures. The only absolute risks by level of use are crude proportions from one cohort; the other absolute figures in the reviews are statements or conditional calculations, not measurements.
